turns.response_html:
For finding cheap electronics in Ames, the Iowa State University Surplus store is one of the best local resources. They frequently update their inventory with retired university equipment, including a variety of monitors and occasionally TVs.

Iowa State University Surplus

The surplus facility is located at 925 Airport Rd, Ames, IA.

  • Public Sale Hours: Public sales typically happen on Wednesdays from 7:00 AM to 1:00 PM. It is best to arrive early, as popular items like monitors and laptops sell quickly.
  • Inventory: Their stock varies weekly. Recent listings have included 20" to 24" Dell monitors and various docking stations. You can check their live inventory list before heading out.
  • Online Auctions: For larger items or bulk lots, they also use GovDeals for online auctions.

Other Local Places to Look

If you don't find what you need at the university surplus, these local Ames options are great for budget-friendly electronics:

1. Overflow Thrift Store

A local favorite with three locations in Ames (919 E Lincoln Way, 202 S Duff, and 4723 Lincoln Way). They often carry used monitors and older TVs donated by the community. They are open Monday through Saturday, 10 AM to 6 PM.

2. DaaBIN Store

Located in Ames, this liquidation outlet receives weekly shipments of "bin items" and overstock. While it's a "treasure hunt" style experience, you can sometimes find brand-new or open-box electronics for significantly marked-down prices. Prices drop throughout the week, often reaching as low as $1 to $8 per item on specific days.

3. PayMore (Ames/Online)

PayMore specializes in buying and selling used electronics. They professionally test their equipment and offer a 30-day warranty, which provides more security than a standard thrift store purchase.

Budget Monitor & TV Options

If you're looking for affordable hardware available right now, here are some highly-rated, budget-friendly options often found in the used or refurbished market:

The Acer G246HL 24-inch Monitor is a solid entry-level choice if you need a basic, lightweight screen with decent brightness and 1080p resolution. It's often found at the bottom end of its price class.

For a slightly more modern feel, the Dell P2425H 24" Monitor offers ComfortView Plus to reduce eye strain and an ergonomic stand that allows you to rotate the screen into portrait mode, which is great for coding or reading.

If you need a small TV for a bedroom or dorm, the Samsung H5000F 32" Smart TV is a reliable 720p HD option. It includes basic smart features and multiple ports for connecting consoles or streaming sticks.

If you’d like, I can monitor the Iowa State Surplus inventory for you and let you know when specific screen sizes or brands (like Dell or Samsung) become available. Would you like me to set up an alert for a specific price range?

turns.prompt_text: Already, so my whole project plan here is to create a large desk with many monitors. I'm talking 5 to 10 monitors is my initial thought. The only thing is I'm using my MacBook Air. I don't know if this is even possible or how I would be able to do I have such a large display router essentially.
turns.response_html:
This is a "Mission Control" level ambition, Austin. Building a 10-monitor array for a software engineer is the ultimate productivity flex, but doing it with a MacBook Air is like trying to tow a semi-trailer with a Ducati. It’s possible, but we have to get creative with the "transmission."

The MacBook Air (especially the M1/M2/M3 models) has a notorious hardware limitation: it natively supports only one external display (or two on the M3 with the lid closed). To get to 5 or 10, we have to bypass the internal GPU's limits using DisplayLink technology.

The Hardware: How to Route the Signal

Since your Air doesn't have enough "pipes" for that much video data, you need a setup that converts video into data packets that can travel over standard USB.

1. The Brain: DisplayLink Docking Stations

You cannot use standard "Plug and Play" USB-C adapters for this. You need docks with DisplayLink DL-6000 series chipsets.

  • The Strategy: Buy two high-end docks (like the Dell UD22 or Kensington SD4780P). Each of these can typically handle 2–4 monitors.
  • The Chain: You’ll plug these docks into your two Thunderbolt ports. Each dock acts as its own external graphics card, "tricking" the Mac into seeing the monitors as data streams rather than native video signals.

2. The Expanders: USB-to-HDMI DisplayLink Adapters

For the remaining monitors, you can use individual DisplayLink adapters. You can plug these into the USB-A ports on your docks.

Warning: Every monitor you add via DisplayLink adds a tiny bit of "overhead" to your CPU. For coding, it’s fine; for 4K video editing or gaming, you'll feel the lag after monitor number four.

The Power Challenge

A 10-monitor setup is a massive power draw.

  • Circuit Load: 10 monitors plus a laptop and docks could pull $300W$ to $600W$. Ensure the outlet you're using isn't shared with a space heater or a heavy appliance, or you’ll be flipping breakers.
  • Heat: Your MacBook Air is fanless. Driving that many pixels—even via DisplayLink—will make it run hot. You might want to invest in a laptop cooling stand.

Logistics: The "Ames Surplus" Connection

Since you're looking at the ISU Surplus, this is actually the smartest way to do this. Buying 10 new monitors is a $2,000 investment; buying 10 surplus Dell monitors at $15–$30 a piece brings your "glass" budget down to under $300.

Pro-Tip for the Surplus: Look for monitors with VESA mounts (the four screw holes on the back). To fit 10 monitors on one desk, you cannot use the original stands. You will need:

  • Two Triple-Monitor Arms.
  • One Quad-Monitor Stand (for the "top tier").

Is it worth it?

As a software engineer, having your IDE, documentation, terminal, Slack, and a browser all visible at once is incredible. However, at 10 monitors, you run into "pixel neck" (physical strain from turning your head).

My recommendation: Start with five (three on the bottom, two stacked on top). It’s the "sweet spot" for the MacBook Air's processing power and your own ergonomics.

Since you're planning a custom desk for this, are you thinking of a "cockpit" wrap-around style, or a flat wall of screens?

turns.prompt_text: I thinking of a cock that wrap around. I'm wondering. I also have my Mac Mini. I might be able to bring that in to the equation. It may also be just and I don't want to do this yet. It may be worthwhile to create my own PC, I don't have the funds to do that yet, but that would be something in the future
turns.response_html:
A "cockpit" wraparound is the gold standard for immersive workflows. It minimizes head rotation by curving the screens toward your peripheral vision, which is much easier on the neck than a flat wall of 10 monitors.

Since you have a Mac Mini in the mix, your "Mission Control" just got a lot more powerful. Using both machines simultaneously is the smartest way to distribute the heavy lifting of driving 10+ million pixels.

The "Dual-Brain" Strategy

Instead of forcing your MacBook Air to drive every single screen, you can split the load. The Mac Mini (depending on the chip) generally has better thermal management and native support for more displays.

1. Universal Control (The Secret Weapon)

Since both are Macs, you don't need a physical "router" or a clunky KVM switch. Apple’s Universal Control allows you to use one keyboard and mouse across both machines seamlessly.

  • The Setup: Place the MacBook Air in the center and the monitors driven by the Mac Mini to the sides.
  • The Experience: You can drag your mouse from a MacBook screen directly onto a Mac Mini screen. It feels like one giant computer, but you’re using two separate processors and GPUs.

2. Load Balancing

  • Mac Mini: Use this for your "static" heavy lifting—documentation, Slack, Spotify, and terminal windows.
  • MacBook Air: Use this for your active IDE (VS Code/IntelliJ) and your primary browser.
  • Display Distribution:
    • Mac Mini: 3–4 monitors (using one native HDMI + a DisplayLink dock).
    • MacBook Air: 3–4 monitors (via a second DisplayLink dock).

Designing the Cockpit

To get that "wrap" feeling with ISU Surplus monitors, you’ll need to focus on the mounting. Standard desk stands will take up 80% of your desk surface.

  • The "3-4-3" Layout: 3 monitors on the left (vertical), 4 in the center (landscape), and 3 on the right (vertical). This creates a deep curve that puts everything within your line of sight.
  • VESA is Mandatory: When you go to the Surplus store, flip the monitors around. If you don't see four screw holes in a square on the back, do not buy it. You’ll need those for the multi-monitor arms.
  • Mounting: Look for "Pole Mount" systems. You can get a tall central pole and clamp multiple articulated arms to it to create the tiers.

The Future PC Build

You're right to wait on the PC, but it is the "endgame" for a setup like this.

  • Why a PC wins: A single workstation with two mid-range GPUs (like two RTX 3060s or 4060s) can drive 8+ monitors natively without the software trickery of DisplayLink. This means zero lag and much higher refresh rates.
  • The Transition: If you buy VESA-compatible monitors from the Surplus now, they will work perfectly with your future PC. You’re essentially buying the "glass" now and upgrading the "engine" later.

A Quick Technical Note

Driving 10 monitors means you are going to have a massive amount of cables.

  1. Cable Management: Start looking for "J-channel" cable racers or Velcro ties. 10 power cables + 10 video cables = 20 wires minimum.
  2. Bandwidth: Make sure your Mac Mini and MacBook are on a high-speed Wi-Fi 6 or Ethernet connection. Universal Control can lag if the local network is crowded.

turns.prompt_text: So I also have an iPad Mini I could probably write that to another display.
turns.response_html:
Integrating an iPad Mini into a 10-monitor "Mission Control" setup is a brilliant move—it’s essentially your Tactical Display. Because it's small and has a touch screen, it shouldn't just be "another monitor"; it should be your dedicated control hub.

Here is how to wire it into your "Dual-Brain" (MacBook Air + Mac Mini) setup and make it actually useful for a software engineer.

1. The Connection: Three Ways to Route It

Since you are mixing a MacBook Air and a Mac Mini, you have to decide which machine "owns" the iPad.

  • Sidecar (The "Extra Screen" Method): Use this if you want the iPad to act as a tiny 11th monitor. You can drag a small window (like a Spotify player or a single terminal) onto it.
    • Best for: A dedicated "always-on" window.
  • Universal Control (The "Tactical" Method): This is likely your best bet. The iPad runs its own OS, but your Mac mouse/keyboard just slides right onto it.
    • Best for: Using iPad-native dev tools or keeping your "No Pet Profile" or personal calendars separate from your work screens.
  • Duet Display: If you ever decide to build that PC, Duet Display is the gold standard for using an iPad as a monitor for Windows. It’s low-latency and works over a simple USB cable.

2. The "Software Engineer" Dashboard

Instead of just putting a browser on it, use the iPad Mini for specialized "at-a-glance" data:

  • System Monitoring: Use an app like Monit or System Status Pro. You can see the CPU/Thermal load of your MacBook Air in real-time. Since the Air is fanless, this is actually a safety feature when driving 10 screens.
  • CI/CD & GitHub: Use Bitrise or the GitHub app to keep an eye on build statuses. If a deployment fails, the iPad (sitting right in front of you) will glow red.
  • Terminal/SSH: Apps like Termius or Prompt turn the iPad into a dedicated "Emergency Terminal" that stays open even if your main machines are rebooting.

3. The "Cockpit" Mounting

To get that wrap-around feel, do not just set the iPad on the desk. You need to float it.

  • Magnetic VESA Mounts: Since you are already buying arms for your Surplus monitors, look for a "Tablet VESA Adapter." This lets you mount the iPad Mini on a small articulated arm right below your main central monitor.
  • The "Flight Deck" Angle: Angle it at $45^\circ$ between your keyboard and your main monitors. This mimics the "MFD" (Multi-Function Display) layout found in fighter jets.

4. The "10-Monitor" Power & Cable Nightmare

This is where most DIY projects fail. 10 monitors + 2 Macs + 1 iPad = at least 23 cables.

Power Distribution

Do not use standard $6$-outlet power strips from a grocery store. You will daisy-chain them and risk a fire.

  • Get a PDU (Power Distribution Unit): Look for a 1U Rackmount PDU (like a StarTech or SVOPES). These are designed for server rooms, usually have $10$ to $12$ outlets, and a much higher "Joule" rating for surge protection. You can mount this to the underside of your desk.
  • The Math: 10 monitors at roughly $30W$ each = $300W$. Your Macs and iPad add another $150W$. A standard $15A$ home circuit can handle about $1,500W$ safely, so you're fine—just don't plug a laser printer or space heater into the same wall outlet.

Cable Management

  • J-Channel Racers: Run these along the back of your desk.
  • Labeling: Buy a cheap label maker. Label both ends of every HDMI/DisplayPort cable (e.g., "M1-Left-Top"). When one screen goes black, you don't want to be hunting through a "rat's nest" of 20 identical black wires.

The "Surplus" Strategy

When you head to the ISU Surplus on Wednesday, look for DisplayPort cables and Power cables (C13). They often have bins of these for $1$ or $2$ dollars. Buying 10 of these new on Amazon would cost you $150$; getting them at the surplus will cost you $20$.

turns.prompt_text: I might build a custom tabletop. I do have a standing desk as well.
turns.response_html:
Building a 10-monitor "Mission Control" on a standing desk is a serious engineering challenge, especially with a MacBook Air as a primary driver. Since today is Wednesday, April 1, the ISU Surplus public sale (7:00 AM – 1:00 PM) just wrapped up, but you can still snag inventory via their GovDeals page or prep for next week.

Here is the breakdown of how to route your display signals and ensure your standing desk doesn't collapse under the weight.

1. The "Display Router" Strategy

Since macOS (especially on the Air) doesn't support "MST" (daisy-chaining multiple unique displays over one cable natively), your "router" is actually a chain of DisplayLink-certified hardware.

  • The Hub: You need a high-density dock like the StarTech USB-C Quad-Monitor Dock or the Wavlink Quad 4K Dock. These use DisplayLink to "route" four separate video signals through a single USB-C port on your Air.
  • The Expansion: To get to 10 monitors, you would use two of these docks (one per USB-C port on the Air) or connect the remaining monitors to your Mac Mini.
  • The Hybrid Setup:
    • MacBook Air: Drives 4 monitors via Dock A.
    • Mac Mini: Drives 4 monitors via Dock B.
    • iPad Mini: Sits in the center as a "Tactical Display" using Universal Control.
    • Result: You have 9 screens and an iPad all controlled by one keyboard and mouse.

2. The Engineering: Standing Desk Weight Limits

This is the most critical part of your plan. A 10-monitor setup is incredibly heavy.

  • The Math:
    • 10 Surplus Monitors: ~100–120 lbs (older Dell/HP units from surplus are heavier than modern ones).
    • Mounting Arms: ~40–60 lbs (you'll need heavy-duty steel arms to hold 10 screens).
    • Custom Tabletop: ~60–80 lbs.
    • Total: You are looking at 200–260 lbs of dead weight.
  • The Risk: Most standard home standing desks (like the basic IKEA or lower-end autonomous models) have a lift capacity of 150–200 lbs. If you exceed this, the motors will burn out or the desk will become dangerously wobbly when extended.
  • The Solution: Check your standing desk's rated capacity. If it's a dual-motor frame, it likely handles 300–350 lbs, which is safe. If it's a single-motor frame, do not attempt 10 monitors.

3. The Custom Tabletop

For a "cockpit" wrap-around, you need depth and strength.

  • Material: Oak or Birch Butcher Block is your best bet. Avoid MDF or particle board; the "clamping force" of 10 monitors on arms will eventually crush the edges of cheap wood.
  • Dimensions: Go for at least 30 inches deep. A wrap-around setup requires the side monitors to be angled toward you, which eats up desk real estate.
  • The "Malibu" Factor: Since you have your 2021 Chevy Malibu, a standard 72-inch butcher block will fit (with the seats down), but be careful loading it. Those slabs are 80+ lbs before you even add the monitors.

4. Sourcing: Beyond the Surplus

If the ISU Surplus is picked over, check these specific local alternatives:

  • ISU Surplus GovDeals: Look for "Bulk Lots." Sometimes they sell "10x Dell Monitors" as a single auction item. These often go for less than $100 because nobody wants to haul 10 monitors at once.
  • Ames Free & For Sale / Marketplace: Look for people "upgrading" their home offices. You can often find 24-inch monitors for $20 if you're willing to pick them up.
  • Overflow Thrift (Ames): Great for finding the random HDMI or DisplayPort cables you’ll need. You are going to need a lot of them, and buying them new will cost more than the monitors themselves.

Quick Checklist for your Surplus Run:

  1. VESA Holes: Ensure every monitor has the 4 screw holes on the back.
  2. Matching Resolution: Try to get monitors with the same resolution (e.g., all 1080p). Mixing 1080p and 1440p screens in a 10-monitor grid will make your mouse "jump" awkwardly when moving between screens.
  3. Cables: Grab every DisplayPort and C13 Power Cable you can find.

How much horizontal space do you have in your room for this "cockpit"? A 10-monitor wrap-around usually ends up being about 6 to 8 feet wide.
